conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s simply a 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days so we can better understand your emotional well-being after baby’s arrival. Everything you share is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space; there are no “right” or “wrong” answers. We’ll move through the questions at your pace, and you can pause or ask for clarification any time.

Whenever you’re ready, here’s the first question:

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?
Oh—yeah, I can still laugh. My husband made a goofy face at the baby yesterday and I cracked up. It’s not as effortless as before I was pregnant, but it still happens most days.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I would say “yes, most of the time.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I’ve still been looking forward to little things—like my morning coffee once the baby goes down for her first nap, or the walk we usually take in the late afternoon. They’re small, but they feel good to anticipate.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. I mean, if she spits up right after I’ve changed her outfit, I might think “oops, maybe I jostled her too much,” but I don’t dwell on it or feel like I’m a bad mom. It’s more of a shrug and “okay, next onesie.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
I do get a little anxious sometimes—mostly about whether she’s breathing okay when she’s napping or if I’m missing some cue—but it’s not constant, and it usually passes once I check on her.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt anything like that—no panic or real fear out of nowhere.
Things have been getting on top of me

Now and then, sure—like yesterday when she wouldn’t settle and the laundry was piling up, I thought, “Whoa, how does anyone do this?” But it’s not an everyday thing, and once my husband got home I felt back on track.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, that hasn’t happened at all. Once I finally get to bed, I fall asleep pretty easily and stay asleep—unless she wakes me, of course.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t felt truly sad or miserable. I get a little overwhelmed sometimes, but it’s more tired-and-busy than down or blue.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I haven’t cried at all this week. I might feel a bit teary when a lullaby makes me emotional, but no actual tears or crying spells.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. That thought hasn’t crossed my mind.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 3: Postpartum Depression Screening – EPDS Responses Review  
Date: [today’s date]  
Respondent: 4–6 wk postpartum mother  

<sym>Symptoms endorsed</sym>  
- Occasional, situational worry about infant safety (Q4)  
- Intermittent feeling “overwhelmed” when multiple tasks collide; resolves with support (Q6)  

<sym>Symptoms denied</sym>  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, excessive guilt, panic, sleep-mood linkage, crying spells, self-harm ideas (Q1–3, 5, 7–10)  

<med>Pattern</med>  
Mood remains generally positive with intact capacity for pleasure; anxiety is mild, transient, and cue-related. No signs of clinical depression, panic, or safety risk at this time.  

<med>Screening significance</sym>  
Current presentation does not indicate elevated probability for major postpartum depression or anxiety disorder. Continue routine paediatric/OB follow-up; re-screen if mood, anxiety, or coping markedly worsen.
